blocks.title: Executive summary
blocks.content:
Over the last 20 years, there has been an increasing realization of the importance of having 
reliable and up-to-date data on the health and care workforce at the national level in order 
to understand the health labour market and to inform the development, implementation and 
review of health workforce (HWF) policies and plans. The Joint Learning Initiative in 2004, 
the World health report in 2006 and the report titled “A universal truth: no health without 
a workforce” in 2013 highlighted the need for countries to invest resources in strengthening 
HWF data and evidence to effectively manag

summary.text: Summarises global progress in National Health Workforce Accounts (NHWA) implementation across 206 countries, territories, and areas (including 98% of WHO Member States), estimating a global health and care workforce of 70.9 million in 2024 and highlighting workforce inequalities and ageing trends through 2030.

blocks.title: Historical overview of health workforce data strengthening efforts
blocks.content:
1.1 Historical overview of health workforce data 
strengthening efforts
Since the onset of the 21st century, there has been an increasing impetus on the central role of 
health workers in developing and ensuring robust health systems and on the need for countries 
to mobilize resources to strengthen their health workforce (HWF), and in particular to generate 
robust HWF data and evidence (Fig. 1). The Joint Learning Initiative – a consortium of more 
than 100 health leaders – recognized in 2004 that the health crisis can only be overcome if 
countries develop national human resources for healt

summary.text: Traces twenty years of global initiatives, World Health Assembly resolutions (including WHA63.16 and WHA69.19), and WHO guidelines from 2004 to 2023 that established and expanded the National Health Workforce Accounts (NHWA) and human resources for health information systems.

blocks.title: What is the NHWA?
blocks.content:
1.2 What is the NHWA?
The NHWA can be defined as a system by which countries progressively improve the availability, 
quality, and use of HWF data through monitoring of a set of indicators to support achievement 
of UHC, SDGs and other health objectives. 
Box 1   Core principles of the NHWA
The core principles of the NHWA are as follows:
•	 Multi-stakeholder and multi-sectoral governance mechanism of the national NHWA data 
•	 System strengthening approach 
•	 Progressive self-paced implementation
•	 Parsimonious approach to collecting validated indicators / proxies
•	 Inclusive country-owned

summary.text: Defines the National Health Workforce Accounts (NHWA) as a country-led system for progressively improving the availability, quality, and use of health workforce data across ten modules following the health labour market framework to support universal health coverage and the SDGs.

blocks.title: About this report
blocks.content:
This report is the inaugural edition of an annual series on the levels and trends of the health 
and care workforce, based on the data shared by countries to WHO through the NHWA, and 
is intended to provide a snapshot of the current and past situation at the global and regional 
levels. This report is also intended for the NHWA focal points, as requested by them during the 
assessment of the NHWA, to advance their understanding of the HWF situation and embrace 
the pertinence of their data sharing.

blocks.title: NHWA data process
blocks.content:
2.1 NHWA data process
Prior to the NHWA process, the WHO Secretariat published annual updates on health workforce 
stock data by health occupations and limited demographics data to the global health workforce 
statistics database, through a data mining process. Currently, at the national level, NHWA focal 
points convene multi-stakeholder and multisectoral (e.g. education, finance, labour, private 
sector) working groups which oversee the collection, collation and analysis of HWF data, by 
following best practices for HRHIS such as diversification of data sources, triangulation of data, 
and d

summary.text: Describes the national and international NHWA data collection, multisectoral collation, triangulation, and validation workflow led by appointed national focal points in collaboration with WHO country, regional, and headquarters teams.

blocks.title: Global and regional estimates
blocks.content:
3.1 Global and regional estimates
Member States have been sharing stock data for several occupations of the health and care 
workforce. Table 1 presents the list of occupational groups in the NHWA data platform, 
along with the frequency of countries which have shared stock data for these occupations. 
Data is available for occupations such as medical doctors, nursing personnel, dentists, 
pharmacists, midwifery personnel, physiotherapists, dental assistants and therapists, dental 
prosthetic technicians, medical imaging and therapeutic equipment technicians, medical 
and pathology laboratory

summary.text: Presents 2024 global, regional, and income-group stock and density estimates totaling 70.9 million health and care workers (15.1 million medical doctors, 31.0 million nursing personnel, 2.3 million midwifery personnel, 2.6 million dentists, 4.1 million pharmacists, and 15.7 million other occupations), highlighting stark regional and income-group disparities.

blocks.title: Global and regional trends
blocks.content:
The density of medical doctors, nursing and midwifery personnel, dentists and pharmacists has 
increased by 52% globally, from 44.8 per 10 000 population reported in 2006 to 67.9 reported in 
2025, with the density of nursing and midwifery personnel increasing by nearly 60% (Table 4). 
Data presented in Table 4 are the estimated densities of the SDG 3.c.1 occupations per 10 000 
population based on the data release for the years 2006, 2012, 2021 and 2025 respectively, and 
hence are to be compared with caution as these estimates were always purely based on the

summary.text: Examines global and regional trends in health workforce stock and density from 2006 to 2025, showing a 52% global increase in the combined density of SDG 3.c.1 occupations from 44.8 to 67.9 per 10 000 population alongside a projected global shortage of 11.1 million health workers by 2030.

This chapter presents an analysis of the joint impact of population and HWF ageing. First, 
demographic statistics on global population ageing are presented, followed by those of health 
workers. The last section shows how both these phenomena would result in a HWF gap under 
a hypothesis of maintaining current (as in 2024) workforce to population density for each age 
group.

blocks.title: Health workforce ageing by occupation
blocks.content:
The age distribution of health workers is linked to the age distribution of the total population, 
showing similarly younger health workers in LICs and older health workers in HICs. However, 
notable differences can be seen when comparing specific occupations, with medical doctors 
being older on average than nursing personnel (Fig. 17 (a) and (b)). This may be attributed to 
the differing education and career pathways for the health occupations.

The global HWF stock is projected to increase faster from 2024 to 2030 (16% increase) than the 
global population during the same period (5% increase). In the European Region and the Region 
of the Americas, where the combined HWF size is higher than other regions, the estimated 
increase of the HWF is smaller (6% in the Region of the Americas and 5% in the European 
Region). Looking at the change in density of health workers between 2024 and the projection 
to 2030 shows that 45 countries are projected to have a lower density by 2030, with 17 of these

summary.text: Projects the 2024–2030 health workforce gap arising from simultaneous population and workforce ageing, finding that 45 countries (including 17 in the WHO European Region) face declining workforce density by 2030 and estimating an additional need for 4.8 million health workers if age-specific utilization is accounted for.

States have appointed focal points for annual reporting to the NHWA platform. Majority of 
countries have reported stock data for multiple occupations, have been reporting stock data 
periodically in the last 7 years, have reported data for various HWF key topics, and this has led 
to a substantial diversification of HWF data be

blocks.title: Annex 3: Methodology to estimate health workforce need
blocks.content:
Methodology to estimate health workforce need
Age-standardization of the health workforce need
In the assessment of the impact of population ageing on the need, an age-standardization 
approach was used. The standardization was a double standardization on population age 
structure and on age-specific medical needs. As a result, the gap between the projected HWF 
by 2030 and the need based on 2020 HWF density was assessed while accounting for a change 
in the density due to change in the age structure of the underlying population.
To illustrate the computation, a country example is provided. In

summary.text: Explains the double age-standardization methodology and country calculation example used to estimate 2030 health workforce requirements accounting for both population age structure shifts and age-specific health care utilization.
